1-2: A runner who overtakes the one in a place takes that place, not the place ahead of it.
Two orders of the same children at once, by height and by age, and a question that mixes them.
Two children of the same height in a chain of comparisons, so that one comparison is a tie.
Two children each taller than a third, so that the shortest is known and the tallest is not.
Seats round a table: who sits on whose left and on whose right.
A see-saw: the heavier child goes down, and two see-saws order three children by weight.
Arrivals by the clock: who came first and who came last from the time each child arrived.
A line that turns round, so that the first becomes the last and every place counts from the other end.
Towers of blocks compared in pairs: which tower is the tallest, and which comes second.
One child leaves a line and joins it again at the end: who is first, and who stands in front of whom now.
3-4: A chain of five comparisons with one given backwards, so that it has to be turned round before it is read.
Places at the finish told by how many runners finished ahead of or behind each one.
A line in which the number of children in front of someone is a given multiple of the number behind.
Known weights or heights matched to names from comparisons, one of them fixed by its number.
A row with exactly some people between two of them, and a second clue that fixes both places.
Overtakings during a race: the places at the finish after a sequence of passes.
Two queues merged into one, each keeping its own order, with clues about who goes before whom.
Seats round a round table: neighbours on the left and on the right, and who sits opposite whom.
A tournament ranked from 'won more games than' clues, with one result given in points.
Four comparisons of which exactly one is false: the order that makes the other three true.
5-6: Places in a contest from statements in which each speaker tells one true half and one false half.
Slots numbered along a rack, with distances between items given counting from both sides.
A queue that changes: people leave, join or swap places, and the order at the end is asked.
Heights or ages given as differences, such as 3 cm taller: the order and the largest gap.
Seats round a circle with clues about neighbours: how many seatings fit every clue.
A ranking rebuilt from the results of every pair in a round-robin tournament.
Two rankings of the same people by two measures, and who stands between whom in both.
A place counted from both ends of a long line, such as fifth from the front and eighth from the back.
The order of events in a day from clues about before, after and at the same time.
The one order that fits every clue, and how many orders fit once one clue is dropped.
